title: Nvidia Ships First H200s to China as Record AI Revenue Doubles
subhead: Nvidia posted a record quarter and confirmed its first H200 data-center chip shipments to China under a new US licensing scheme, ending a months-long lockout. Meanwhile SK Hynix broke ground on its first US HBM plant and China's Zhipu ran a viral model entirely on domestic chips.

sections.heading: Nvidia's Record Quarter Opens a Narrow China Door
sections.body:
Nvidia reported net income of $59.69 billion on revenue of $96.22 billion for the May-July quarter, more than doubling revenue from a year earlier and beating the $92.27 billion consensus, according to Nikkei Asia and AP. The data-center segment alone brought in $89 billion, up more than twofold. The company forecast about $108 billion in revenue for the current quarter, an 89% year-on-year jump, and said it expects roughly 70% growth in its 2028 fiscal year, describing the outlook as supply-constrained.

The strategic shift came on China: Nvidia confirmed its first shipments of H200 data-center processors to China under a new US licensing scheme, ending a months-long lockout, per SCMP. The sales accounted for less than 1% of the $89 billion data-center total. Washington approved H200 exports in January, but Beijing initially restricted purchases to promote domestic alternatives before allowing selected Chinese AI firms to buy limited quantities last month. Nvidia's outlook still assumes no data-center computing revenue from China.
sections.whyItMatters: The H200 shipments are a calibrated reopening of the US-China AI chip trade — enough to keep Chinese firms buying Nvidia, but small enough that Nvidia's growth story no longer depends on China at all. It signals Washington and Beijing are managing a controlled thaw rather than a full re-engagement.

sections.heading: SK Hynix Breaks Ground on First US HBM Plant as Memory Crunch Extends
sections.body:
SK Hynix officially broke ground Thursday on its first US plant for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in West Lafayette, Indiana, a project worth more than $4 billion that includes an advanced chip-packaging facility and an R&D complex near Purdue University, Nikkei Asia reports. The plant will assemble next-generation HBM4E memory onshore for American customers.

CEO Kwak Noh-Jung said he sees 'no signal' of oversupply risk and expects the global memory shortage to last until the end of 2030, arguing memory chips are 'no longer just commodities' in the AI era. The buildout is part of a broader wave: Kioxia plans to invest about $6.27 billion in a new memory facility in northern Japan, following Samsung and SK Hynix, while YMTC's parent CCSH is seeking a $4.9 billion Shanghai IPO on the AI memory boom.
sections.whyItMatters: Moving HBM packaging to US soil is a direct answer to the chokepoint that memory packaging represents in the AI supply chain. With SK Hynix, Samsung and Kioxia all expanding and YMTC raising capital, the memory race is now explicitly a geopolitical one — onshore capacity in the US and Japan versus a capitalizing Chinese challenger.

sections.heading: Zhipu Runs Viral Model Entirely on Chinese Chips
sections.body:
China's Zhipu AI launched its open-weight GLM-5.3-Flash model — previously code-named Ox Alpha — saying it ran entirely on a cluster of 100,000 domestically produced chips during a stealth trial, SCMP reports. The model processed 62 trillion tokens before its formal release Wednesday, and more than 11 trillion tokens in its first three days on the OpenRouter marketplace, making it the platform's biggest launch to date. Zhipu's shares closed more than 12% higher in Hong Kong.

The release is a demonstration that Chinese AI can scale on domestic silicon as Beijing pushes to cut reliance on US hardware. It follows a week in which the model ranked first among coding systems on OpenRouter, accounting for nearly 31% of the platform's weekly token volume.
sections.whyItMatters: A 100,000-chip domestic cluster running a top-ranked coding model is the strongest public evidence yet that China's export-control workaround is maturing. It does not erase the performance gap with Nvidia, but it narrows the practical dependence and gives Beijing a credible domestic alternative to point to.

sections.heading: Alibaba Launches Brazil Data Centres in Emerging-Market AI Push
sections.body:
Alibaba Group launched its first data centres in South America, a Brazilian venture operating two facilities offering local enterprises cloud infrastructure and 'agentic AI services', SCMP reports. Alibaba Cloud now claims a presence in 106 availability zones across 31 regions, following its first Latin American facility in Mexico in early 2025.

The move is part of Alibaba's rapid AI infrastructure buildout outside mainland China as it seeks growth markets amid the US-China AI rivalry. The company said the local infrastructure gives Brazilian enterprises, start-ups and public institutions direct access to cloud services engineered for low latency and data governance.
sections.whyItMatters: China's cloud giants are competing for emerging-market AI infrastructure before US providers consolidate their grip. Brazil is a test of whether Chinese AI infrastructure can win sovereign and enterprise workloads in markets wary of both US and Chinese dominance.

sections.heading: White House Bans Foreign-Made Power Equipment Over Backdoor Fears
sections.body:
The Trump administration issued an executive order banning the acquisition of foreign-made technology used to manage electricity and power, citing concerns that bulk-power system equipment may contain digital backdoors allowing foreign governments remote access or supply-chain disruption, The Record reports. The order declares a national emergency to secure the US bulk-power system.

It follows a string of critical-infrastructure attacks: water utilities in at least 12 states experienced cyberattacks last month, and CISA said it observed malicious activity targeting over 100 internet-exposed systems in the water and wastewater sector. In the UK, hackers reportedly shut down a small power plant for four days. While no countries were officially blamed, several experts pointed to Iranian hackers.
sections.whyItMatters: The order formalizes a supply-chain security doctrine for the power grid, effectively barring Chinese and other foreign vendors from a core US infrastructure market. It is a concrete regulatory escalation of the hardware-trust debate that has been building around critical infrastructure.

sections.heading: Finland Revives Eagle S Cable Case, Closing a Jurisdiction Gap
sections.body:
A Finnish appeals court revived the prosecution of three senior officers of the Eagle S, the Russia-linked oil tanker that severed multiple subsea cables in the Baltic Sea on Christmas Day 2024, The Record reports. The Helsinki Court of Appeal ruled Finland has jurisdiction to try the men, overturning a district court decision that had thrown out the case last October.

The court held the alleged crimes were committed in Finland because the damage and its effects on the country's power and telecommunications supply occurred there, and ruled the events did not amount to a 'maritime accident' under UNCLOS — the provision the defense had used to argue the case belonged in the ship's flag state, the Cook Islands. The case returns to the Helsinki District Court, though the three men have left Finland.
sections.whyItMatters: The ruling closes a legal loophole that maritime lawyers warned would let flag-of-convenience ships damage undersea infrastructure in international waters with impunity. It strengthens the legal basis for holding crews accountable for cable sabotage, a growing concern for European digital and energy security.

sections.heading: German Firms Report Surge in State-Sponsored Cyberattacks
sections.body:
Nearly four in 10 German companies hit by data theft, industrial espionage or sabotage in the past year attributed at least one incident to a foreign intelligence service, up from 28% last year and just 7% in 2023, according to a Bitkom survey of 1,003 companies reported by The Record. China was the most frequently cited foreign source, with Russia second and Iran emerging as a significant source.

Bitkom estimated cyberattacks cost German businesses between $186 billion and $240 billion over the past year. Germany's domestic intelligence chief Sinan Selen said foreign intelligence services have 'intensified their hybrid activities,' with the security and defense industry a particularly attractive target.
sections.whyItMatters: The sharp year-on-year jump in state-attributed attacks shows espionage is becoming a mainstream cost of doing business in Europe, and that the line between criminal gangs and state agencies is blurring. It reinforces the case for tighter supply-chain and operational security across European industry.

bottomLine: Today's defining development is the controlled reopening of the US-China AI chip trade: Nvidia posted a record quarter and shipped its first H200s to China under a new licensing scheme, but still assumes no data-center revenue from China — a sign both sides are managing a narrow, reversible thaw. In parallel, the memory and packaging race is going onshore, with SK Hynix breaking ground on its first US HBM plant and Kioxia expanding in Japan, while China's Zhipu demonstrated a top-ranked model running on 100,000 domestic chips. On the security side, the US banned foreign-made power equipment over backdoor concerns, Finland revived the Eagle S cable case, and German firms reported a surge in state-sponsored attacks. The through-line is a world hardening its tech supply chains on every axis — chips, memory, power equipment and undersea cables — even as the AI trade itself reopens selectively.
sources: Nikkei Asia, AP, SCMP, The Record (Recorded Future News), Bitkom
